meta_title: Pharos — open, honest science against authoritarianism
meta_description: Pharos is a free, open observatory of democratic resilience: an honest record of what research shows about authoritarianism, a measurement of how governance is changing across ~204 countries, and the exact conditions that would change our minds. Watch power, not people.
og_title: Pharos — science against authoritarianism, with the uncertainty in the headline
og_description: A free, open evidence commons: {{within_noise_pct}}% of a decade's measured governance change is within measurement noise — and we lead with that. Graded, falsifiable, reproducible offline. Watch power, not people.
eyebrow: A free, open project · for the public
subtitle: Science against authoritarianism
lede: A free, open observatory of how democracies are doing — built on published data, with the uncertainty in the headline, not the footnote: {{within_noise_pct}}% of a decade of measured governance change is within measurement noise.
rule: Built in the open. Cited only to what is measured. Bound by one rule: watch power, not people.
cta_primary: What it is, in plain words
plain_p1: Pharos is a public project that does two things. It keeps an honest record of what research shows about authoritarianism — how it grows, what feeds it, how societies have resisted it — and it measures how democratic governance is changing around the world, from published data, keeping the error bars. Everything is open: the data, the code, the reasoning and the corrections.
plain_p2: It is a lighthouse, not a dragnet: it watches governments and institutions, never individuals. The project collects nothing about its readers — no account, no analytics, no scripts on this page — and the full project runs on your own computer, offline.
plain_p3: It is for anyone who wants a sober read instead of panic or denial — citizens; journalists, teachers and students who need checkable sources; researchers and developers who want to reproduce, challenge or build on the results.
not_prediction: Not a prediction machine. Its forecast of democratic backsliding does not yet beat the simplest guess — “nothing changes” — and it says so (see § 05).
not_surveillance: Not a surveillance tool. No person-level data is published, and a build gate fails on any data below country level (§ 07).
not_partisan: Not partisan. The unit of study is the mechanism — how erosion and resistance spread — not any party, country or leader.
not_finished: Not finished. Version {{version}}, unfunded and independent; the commitments still open are listed in STATUS.md.
evidence_intro: We measured democratic governance across six World Bank dimensions for ~204 countries, 2014–2024 — and we kept the uncertainty. The honest headline is narrower, and more useful, than the doom-or-denial you usually read:
finding_sub: of ~1,200 country-by-dimension changes are within measurement noise — most of the world did not measurably move in a decade.
bar_label: Of all governance changes: {{within_noise_pct}}% within measurement noise, about {{decline_pct_round}}% real declines, about {{improve_pct_round}}% real improvements.
finding_note: Of the changes that are real, the erosion is concentrated in one place: Voice & Accountability — free expression, free media, participation, the accountability of power.
evidence_p2: We flag a change only when it beats its 90% confidence interval — and the voice decline survives the stricter 95% bar too. And we don’t ask you to trust one number: we put the same question to three instruments (the World Bank, V-Dem, and Freedom House — overlapping, not independent: V-Dem feeds the World Bank’s aggregate) and publish where they agree and where they conflict. Every instrument that registers a significant change concurs on a decline in voice in {{concur_decline}} countries — none dissenting, and in {{concur_decline_full3}} of them all three are significant on their own; the handful where they genuinely disagree are flagged as conflicts, never averaged into a false consensus. A gamed single non-overlapping source surfaces as a conflict, not a clean number.
fold_method_summary: How the measurement works — in one paragraph
fold_method_p: For each country and governance dimension, we take the change in the published 0–100 score from 2014 to 2024. The World Bank publishes a 90% confidence interval with every score; from it we derive the standard error and test the change with a two-sided z-test, flagging decline or improvement only when the change exceeds what the combined measurement uncertainty allows. Deliberately conservative: anything smaller stays unflagged, because it could be noise. The voice finding is stress-tested twice more — it survives the stricter 95% bar and an alternative time window — and the full method, code, and data ship in the repository, reproducible offline with one command.
inside_intro: An open, reproducible evidence commons — not a dashboard of opinions. Every claim carries its grade and the exact condition under which it would be withdrawn.
card_ledger_p: {{ledger_entries}} graded, falsifiable evidence entries — {{robust}} ROBUST · {{contested}} CONTESTED · {{refuted}} REFUTED · {{open}} OPEN — each with a pre-registered falsification trigger and a machine-checked structure. A generated falsification watch gathers every trigger in one place, and each entry’s next-review date goes stale loudly, not silently.
card_indicators_p: Governance change across six dimensions, computed with honest uncertainty, with Voice & Accountability triangulated against V-Dem and Freedom House to publish divergence, never a single score.
card_forecast_p: A calibration layer, not a hero call: pre-registered backsliding forecasts, scored against a no-change baseline — honest enough to tell you it doesn’t beat that baseline yet (see § 05).
card_sims_p: Seven validated mechanisms of social change — each reproduces a published result via a unit test (threshold and network cascades, the committed-minority tipping point, reverse dominance, complex contagion, the legitimacy tipping point, and bounded-confidence opinion dynamics).
card_audit_p: Every headline figure is machine-checked — structure, freshness, an overstatement guard, a count-consistency gate, and a spatial-floor gate that fails the build on data columns or labels below country level — all reproducible offline, one command, no network. Beyond the gates, the whole corpus has been put through adversarial review: every citation web-verified, every load-bearing formula independently re-implemented (5 of 6 bit-exact; the sixth exposed a rounding bug, since fixed).
card_tested_p: A tiering map of every load-bearing claim, from machine-verified down to honestly untestable. Nothing claims a tier it hasn’t earned.
fold_grades_summary: What the grades mean — and what would change our minds
grade_robust_d: Verified against primary sources; uncontested, or convergent across independent lines of evidence.
grade_contested_d: Real evidence on both sides — replication failures or unresolved expert dispute. Reported as live, not settled.
grade_refuted_d: Fails verification. Kept on the record so no one builds on it twice.
grade_open_d: The evidence does not yet answer the question — and we say so.
grades_p: Every entry also pre-registers its falsification trigger — the specific observation that would downgrade it. Meet a trigger with evidence and the grade moves: in public, dated, and credited. That is the difference between an evidence commons and advocacy.
fold_check_summary: How to check us — without trusting us
fold_check_p1: Trust should be checkable, not requested. The signals, each verifiable on your own machine, offline: self-correction on the record — a REFUTED grade kept in public view, a forecast whose published headline is its own negative result, and adversarial review rounds whose findings against our own work are documented with their fixes. Byte-exact reproduction — one command recomputes everything from pinned snapshots with no network and fails on drift between code, data, and the pinned figures in the prose. Pre-registered falsifiability — every entry’s “what would change our minds” collected in one watchlist. Uncertainty as the headline — the noise floor is the most prominent number we publish, and disagreement between instruments is surfaced, never blended. No funder to please — currently unfunded and independent; if that ever changes, disclosure comes first.
fold_check_p2: The full list, one verification command per signal, ships in the repo as docs/TRUST_SIGNALS.md. The one-command version: make verify-offline.
fold_demo_summary: The method, demonstrated on someone else’s claims
fold_demo_p: We hold the same bar to ourselves and to others — adversarial, steelmanned, graded. As a worked example, we ran the verification on a famous set of public claims: of Graham Hancock’s ten major claims, 0 were supported and 5 refuted — while fairly crediting the few real things mainstream science has had to update on. The discipline, not the verdict, is the product.
use_intro: Three ways in, from no installation to full verification. Nothing here needs an account, and nothing phones home.
download_p: One small file with everything: the evidence ledger, the data, the code, the documents and the local observatory — free, under open licences, no account needed. Unzip it anywhere; there is no installer. Prefer git? git clone {{url_repo}}. Or browse every file on GitHub without downloading anything.
path_read_p: No installation. Start with the plain-language brief — what the data says, in ordinary words. Browse the evidence ledger: every entry by grade, each linked to its sources, and every “what would change our minds” trigger in one place. The watch report (a prototype) lists the countries where all three instruments concur that civic voice declined. The README routes you by what you came for.
path_run_p: The interactive observatory runs on your own machine, offline. It needs only Python 3.9 or newer — free from python.org, and most Linux systems already have it. Nothing else to install.
step_download: Download the project: as a ZIP file (then unzip it), or with git clone {{url_repo}}.
step_serve: Open a terminal in the project folder and run python3 src/pharos.py serve — on Windows, py src\pharos.py serve.
step_open: Open http://127.0.0.1:8796/ in your browser. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.
path_run_more: The same program has a text mode. On macOS and Linux, ./pharos is its shortcut: ./pharos brief prints the plain-language read, ./pharos ledger browses the entries, ./pharos watch lists every falsification trigger, ./pharos stats gives a one-glance summary. The full guide: docs/LOCAL_OBSERVATORY.md.
path_check_p: From a git clone, make verify-offline recomputes every indicator and the forecast from the pinned data, with no network, and fails on any drift from the published numbers; make dashboard prints one GREEN/RED report across the audits. If the freshness check fails, a ledger entry is overdue for review — that alarm is by design. To contribute, read CONTRIBUTING.md: the most valuable contribution is meeting a claim’s falsification trigger with evidence, and the falsification-challenge issue template walks you through it. Fixing a citation, adding a test or improving a translation are welcome too.
forecast_p1: Anyone can publish a scary prediction. The hard, trustworthy thing is to score yourself in the open. So the forecasting pillar runs {{n_forecasts_fmt}} pre-registered backsliding forecasts — a backtest over 2000–2014 origins, its design fixed before scoring — and grades them with proper scoring rules against two dead-simple baselines — assume no change, or just predict the long-run base rate — then reports the result plainly:
forecast_quote: Our models beat neither baseline yet — and we say so, in public.
forecast_p2: That isn’t a weakness to bury; it is the product. The bar to clear is written down before the scoring, and a future model earns its place only by beating it on the same open harness. A project that will tell you when its own forecast isn’t good enough is one you can believe when it says something is.
h_how: How it works — the lighthouse, not the dragnet
how_p: Durable change can come when a committed minority reaches a critical mass and a cascade spreads — but that cascade runs on trusted, reinforcing signal, exactly what disinformation destroys. So we don’t aggregate or surveil people. We build a true, open, reusable thing that aligned people find and gather around, voluntarily. Supplying a missing, trusted information feedback loop — what open, falsifiable science is — is a foundation a small team can actually build; it crosses into action only once it is also made salient and taken up in real work. It is a necessary seed, not a sufficient cause: organizing and solidarity are coequal, never downstream.
rule_p: Everything here measures the conduct of institutions and power — never individuals. No surveillance, no predictive policing, no targeting. An instrument built to defend open societies must never become one that could serve their enemies. And because a covenant alone is non-binding on open licences, it is backed by a threat model with an enforced part: a build gate scans every published data file and fails on columns or labels below country level, so protection lives in the design, not just the promise. Its per-release checklist, including a red-team of the published forecasts, is still open (see STATUS.md).
open_p1: Multi-licensed and reproducible: prose under CC BY-SA 4.0, code under GPL-3.0-or-later, derived data under CC0. The whole project runs as one stdlib-only command — offline, no install, no network — recomputes from pinned data and self-audits before every change. Fork it, check it, build on it, prove it wrong. The strongest contribution is meeting a claim’s falsification trigger with evidence.
open_p2: Everything lives in one public repository, github.com/LX8/pharos. This page is published from it in English, Spanish, German and Portuguese: all four versions are generated from one template and the same data, and a check fails the build if a translation’s numbers, links or commands differ from the English page’s.
sources_intro: The primary sources behind this page — every one verified against the published record before being cited (the full, per-claim source lists live with each ledger entry):
ref_wgi: World Bank — Worldwide Governance Indicators (the six dimensions, with published confidence intervals).
ref_owid: V-Dem — freedom-of-expression index, and Freedom House — civil liberties, both via Our World in Data (the triangulation instruments).
ref_views: Hegre, H. et al. (2019). ViEWS: a political violence early-warning system. Journal of Peace Research.
ref_views2: Hegre, H. et al. (2024). The 2023/24 VIEWS Prediction Challenge — forecasts scored as full distributions by CRPS; whether models beat a no-change baseline is metric- and task-dependent (ledger entry SAA-040), which is why our forecast is scored against that baseline.
ref_gneiting: Gneiting, T. & Raftery, A. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. JASA (the CRPS our forecast is scored by).
ref_paxton: Paxton, R. O. (2004). The Anatomy of Fascism. Knopf (the behavioral definition this project uses).
ref_bermeo: Bermeo, N. (2016). On Democratic Backsliding. Journal of Democracy (erosion as gradual executive aggrandizement, not coups).
ref_sims: Granovetter, M. (1978) AJS; Watts, D. J. (2002) PNAS; Centola, D. & Macy, M. (2007) AJS; Xie, J. et al. (2011) Phys. Rev. E; Johnson & MacKay (2015) Evolution & Human Behavior; Deffuant, G. et al. (2000) Adv. Complex Syst.; Fortunato (2004) Int. J. Mod. Phys. C; Epstein, J. (2002) PNAS — the published results the mechanism simulators reproduce. Centola, D. et al. (2018) Science is the experimental contrast (a tipping point of about 25%, measured in people).
ref_wineburg: Wineburg, S. & McGrew, S. (2019). Lateral Reading and the Nature of Expertise. Teachers College Record (the actionable epistemic defense).
